summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Depression is heterogeneous and dynamic, and changes in observable behavior may accompany some of its clinical manifestations. Digital devices offer new opportunities to capture this behavior in naturalistic settings continuously. However, the specific digital features captured through device interactions and their relationships to depression-related outcomes have yet to be synthesized, and their potential relevance to functional constructs is unclear. The research domain criteria (RDoC) may provide a conceptual framework for exploring potential links between digital behaviors and functional constructs. <strong>Objective:</strong> This scoping review aimed (1) to identify and summarize key online behavioral modalities and their specific features for depression monitoring and assessment, (2) to summarize existing evidence on associations between specific behavioral features and depression-related outcomes, and (3) to explore whether the behavioral content captured by digital measures has the potential conceptual links to RDoC constructs. <strong>Methods:</strong> We conducted a scoping review of 5 databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and PsycINFO) from inception through January 2026, supplemented by citation tracking and gray literature searches. Included studies focused on online behavioral digital phenotyping for depression and reported specific behavioral features. Two reviewers (QR and JC) independently screened studies and extracted data, with disagreements resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer (YH). Findings were synthesized descriptively. Two reviewers (QR and Kaili Tang) independently assessed potential conceptual links between each behavioral modality and RDoC constructs using the official RDoC construct definitions. <strong>Results:</strong> In total, 74 studies were included. Five primary behavioral modalities were identified: call behavior (n=31), SMS (n=21), screen use (n=41), app use (n=26), and keystroke dynamics (n=14), comprising 36 core features. A total of 31 (41.9%) studies reported findings attributable to individual features, but no single feature showed a consistently directed association with depression-related outcomes across studies. An exploratory RDoC assessment suggested that candidate construct relevance primarily involved social processes, sensorimotor systems, cognitive systems, and arousal and regulatory systems. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Online behavioral digital phenotyping captures a range of observable behaviors, but current evidence does not support interpreting individual digital behavioral features as stable markers of depression or as direct proxies for specific RDoC constructs. Future research should improve the transparency of feature definitions and reporting, strengthen the reporting of feature-level findings, and use independent validation and construct-informed study designs to enhance interpretability.
title: Online Behavioral Digital Phenotyping for Depression: Scoping Review of Behavioral Features and Exploratory Assessment of Research Domain Criteria Construct Relevance

summary: Background: The rise of online mental health communities has reshaped the ways individuals seek and receive mental health support. Although online mental health communities (OMHCs) offer a valuable space for peer support, including through experience-sharing, they also present challenges, including moderation practices to cultivate supportive interactions and secure member safety. No comprehensive framework of moderation practices has been established. Developing such an understanding is important, as moderators play a central role in facilitating a sense of community and determining whether OMHCs function as safe and supportive spaces. Objective: This study aimed to develop typologies of moderator practices used to support safety and facilitate a sense of community within OMHCs for people with mental health problems, and the content of OMHC community guidelines. Methods: A systematized review of empirical research studies focusing on moderation practices and community guidelines in OMHCs was conducted using MEDLINE, Web of Science, Association for Computing Machinery Digital Library, supplemented with a purposive search to identify gray literature on community guidelines for OMHC moderation. Inclusion criteria: online, text-based component, asynchronous or synchronous moderation, mental health–related focus, and human moderation. Exclusion criteria: crisis-focused, audience-based, nonmoderated or bot-moderated, profession not peer support, non-English, and academic review or thesis. The search period was 2014 to 2024. A bespoke data extraction sheet was piloted, then populated, capturing document, OMHC, member, and moderator characteristics. Thematic analysis was used to synthesize the findings relating to each objective. Results: The systematized search identified 11,347 studies and other documents, from which 80 studies were included, comprising 48 empirical papers and 32 gray literature documents. These related to 52 different OMHCs. Four categories of moderator practices were identified: (1) premoderation and postmoderation processes, (2) reactive moderation processes, (3) building the community, and (4) monitoring members. Premoderation and postmoderation processes were used within 41 (79%) of the 52 OMHCs. Three categories of community guideline content were identified: (1) content of post, (2) member conduct, and (3) moderation. The category, content of post, was the most widely used component of community guidelines, used in 35 (67%) of the 52 OMHCs. Conclusions: The two typologies provide a foundational framework that can be adapted and applied to community guidelines and moderation strategies across a range of contexts. When operationalized, they could provide benefit to people with mental health problems by using them to guide the development of moderator training, digital tools, and governance policies that align with the specific characteristics and objectives of individual OMHCs. Effective translation and application of these typologies require careful, nuanced consideration of each community’s goals, membership, and cultural context to ensure their relevance, effectiveness, and impact.
title: A Typology of Moderator Practices and Community Guidelines in Online Mental Health Communities to Establish a Framework for Digital Safety: Systematized Review

summary: Background: Smart care robots are increasingly viewed as a potential way to address care burden and support care quality in long-term care facilities. However, their integration into routine care practice remains limited, and the conditions required for their effective implementation are not yet well understood from the perspective of frontline nursing assistants. Objective: This study aimed to clarify nursing assistants’ core functional expectations of smart care robots in long-term care facilities and to explore the key conditions for their integration into practice. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study was conducted. Using purposive sampling, 31 frontline nursing assistants were recruited from 5 long-term care facilities in Chengdu, Sichuan Province, China, with recruitment assistance from facility administrators and eligibility screening by the research team. Semistructured face-to-face interviews were conducted between September and November 2025. Data were analyzed using framework analysis. Results: Framework analysis produced 4 analytical domains: real-world care needs, limited facilitating conditions, major anticipated barriers, and preparatory pathways for implementation. Participants expected robots to support safety monitoring and risk warning, standardized checking and management, repetitive physical tasks, and basic interaction. Although some openness to technology and organizational support existed, these facilitating conditions were insufficient for routine implementation. Key barriers included unclear human-robot collaboration models, inadequate organizational capacity, potential new care risks, and weak external support. Participants emphasized organizational assessment, contextual adaptation, pilot testing, and structured training as essential preparatory steps. Emotional support functions were also valued for alleviating caregivers’ emotional burden in high-intensity care work. Conclusions: Openness to technology, supportive organizational climates, and positive policy and social signals provided an initial foundation for considering robot integration. However, uncertainties remained around human-robot collaboration, risk management, organizational capacity, and concrete external support. Organizational assessment, contextual adaptation, real-world pilot testing, and practical training warrant further evaluation before wider implementation.
title: Conditions and Pathways for Integrating Smart Care Robots Into Long-Term Care Facilities: Qualitative Study From Nursing Assistants’ Perspectives

summary: Background: Use of secure messaging within the patient portal has grown rapidly over recent years, yet clinical workflows, staffing models, and billing practices have generally not been comprehensively adapted to support this increasing volume of messages. Little is known about the characteristics of patients who are high-volume message senders, and we lack a nuanced understanding of patient messaging intensity beyond measures accounting for sheer volume, limiting health system efforts to anticipate message-related workflow demands and allocate resources effectively. Objective: Our objective was to characterize older adult patients (aged ≥65 years) with high secure messaging volume, examining both patient characteristics and other aspects of their messaging intensity, such as messaging frequency, length, and messaging use relative to patient portal logins and health care encounters. Methods: We analyzed electronic medical record and patient portal data from a large academic health system, encompassing 16,023 older adults who sent 199,981 messages over a 12-month period. We developed 5 measures to account for secure messaging intensity. Our primary measure of messaging intensity was based on message volume; high-volume message senders were identified using outlier analysis based on patients’ aggregate number of messages sent during the observation period. Additional measures of messaging intensity included identifying individuals with concentrated periods of messaging, message length (character count), a ratio of messages to portal logins, and a ratio of messages to health care encounters. We compared sociodemographic characteristics, health status, and messaging intensity of high-volume secure messaging senders with those of other message senders. Results: Of 16,023 older adult patients who sent at least 1 message during the observation period, 1298 (8.1%) were classified as high-volume message senders; these patients accounted for 39.7% (79,475/199,981) of total messages. High-volume message senders, compared with all other message senders, were more likely to be White (1044/1298, 80.4% vs 10,670/14,725, 72.5%; <.001), have higher comorbidity scores (2.6 vs 1.8; <.001), and higher incidence of cancer (465/1298, 35.8% vs 3354/14,725, 22.8%; <.001) and dementia (107/1298, 8.2% vs 889/14,725, 6.1%; <.002). High-volume message senders were also more likely to be identified as having concentrated periods of messaging, to send longer messages, and to send more messages in relation to patient portal logins and health care encounters. Conclusions: High-volume message senders represent a small but distinct group of older patients who send a large share of messages to clinicians. Using multiple measures of messaging intensity can provide additional context about patient messaging behavior and help health systems redesign workflows and care delivery models to meet patient communication needs while facilitating sustainable workloads for clinicians.
title: The Role of Measurement in Identifying High-Intensity Secure Message Senders Among Older Adults: Observational Study

summary: Background: Globally, the carbon footprint of the health care sector is significant and growing, and digital health care technologies (DHTs) offer unique opportunities to reduce the carbon footprint of health and care systems. However, their environmental impact has not been adequately investigated. Objective: This scoping review aims to explore the environmental impact of DHTs, focusing on reducing their carbon footprint and evaluating methods for assessing that impact. Methods: This scoping review followed the method outlined by Arksey and O’Malley, adhering to the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. The databases of MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for studies published in English with no time limitation. Search terms were categorized under three broader concepts: “Digital Health Technologies,” “Health and Care,” and “Carbon Footprint.” Studies were included based on screening titles and abstracts, followed by review of full-text papers by at least 2 reviewers. Narrative synthesis was used to report the findings. Results: The database search yielded 4274 studies. Following screening and reference list checks, 70 studies were selected for inclusion. The earliest included study was published in 2007, with the majority originating from the United States (n=26) and the United Kingdom (n=12). Most studies assessed telemedicine or telehealth interventions. Retrospective analyses predominated, although prospective, cross-sectional, mixed method, and life cycle assessment (LCA) designs were also reported. Environmental impact was most often evaluated through travel-related carbon savings, with some studies incorporating energy use, medical equipment or resources, infrastructure, or waste. LCA studies applied process-based approaches that included detailed activity- and product-specific data, as well as Environmentally Extended Input-Output (EEIO) models. In most cases, carbon footprint measurements were based on assumptions, with calculations relying on published emission factors or calculators. Some studies have expressed CO emissions using emission equivalencies, such as equivalent carbon sequestration and equivalent CO emissions. Overall, DHTs demonstrated positive environmental impacts by reducing carbon footprint. However, negative impacts, especially electricity consumption and the lifecycle impacts of digital devices, were also noted. Conclusions: DHTs are associated with reductions in carbon emissions and related environmental benefits, with telemedicine showing potential to lower the carbon footprint of the health care sector. However, evidence highlights the negative impacts associated with energy demand and the full lifecycle of digital devices. Given the substantial heterogeneity in assessment methods and outcome measures across studies, these findings should be interpreted with caution. To capture the true environmental implications of digital health, more rigorous, standardized, and comprehensive assessment methods are required. Bridging these methodological gaps is essential to ensure that DHTs not only support sustainable health care delivery but also make a meaningful contribution to mitigating global climate change. Trial Registration: OSF Registries osf.io/gdnve; https://osf.io/gdnve/overview
title: Environmental Impact of Digital Health Care Technologies in Reducing Carbon Footprints: Scoping Review

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Patient access to their electronic health records (EHRs) could improve care and reduce errors by enabling patient contribution to documentation. However, interactive functions that support such engagement remain underresearched. <strong>Objective:</strong> The purpose of this study was to analyze patients’ use of the free-text comment function in the Swedish national patient-accessible EHR. <strong>Methods:</strong> Comments made by patients between 2015 and 2021 for health care professionals to view were retrieved from the patient-accessible EHR administration service in Sweden. The number and length of comments were analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests, while the content was examined qualitatively using inductive content analysis. In addition, comments were coded for sentiment (positive, neutral, or negative) and note content, and users were classified according to whether they had submitted at least 1 comment referring to mental health care. <strong>Results:</strong> A total of 1670 comments were left by 659 patients, of which 15 had irrelevant content (15/1670, 0.9%; 95% CI 0.4%-1.4%), leaving 1655 comments for analysis. Most comments (948/1655, 57.3%; 95% CI 54.9%-59.7%) were related to matters other than note content, and nearly all had a neutral (920/1655, 55.6%; 95% CI 53.2%-58.0%) or negative (702/1655, 42.4%; 95% CI 40.0%-44.8%) sentiment. Patients who submitted a comment referencing mental health care tended to leave more comments overall (median 7 vs 2 comments per patient), and their comments were more frequently negative than comments written by other patients (313/495, 63.2% vs 389/1160, 33.5%; <i>P</i><.001). The most prevalent categories were care engagement, perceived inaccuracies, complaints, and requests. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Patient engagement with clinical notes has the potential to enhance documentation accuracy and strengthen patient-clinician communication. To realize these benefits safely, such features must be deliberately designed and clearly explained to users to avoid patient safety risks and unnecessary burdens on health care professionals.
title: Patient Use of a Comment Function in Electronic Health Records: Mixed Methods Case Study

summary: Background: Engagement with suicide-related content online is often assumed to be harmful, yet many individuals with lived experience describe such content as supportive or even life-preserving. Despite policy and clinical concerns, little is known about how people intentionally or unintentionally encounter this content, how they interpret it, and how these experiences shape perceived harm or benefit. Objective: This study aims to explore how intent and context influence the ways in which individuals with lived experience of suicidality encounter, interpret, and respond to suicide-related online content, and to identify factors associated with perceived harm and benefit. Methods: An exploratory cross-sectional survey was conducted with a convenience sample of 713 UK-based participants aged 16 to 60 years and older, 95.9% (n=684) of whom reported having lived experience of suicidality. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, including chi-square tests, to examine associations between engagement patterns, intent, and suicidality. Free-text responses were coded using content analysis to identify categories relating to motivations for engagement, emotional responses, and perceived impact. Results: Participants reported a broad range of experiences. While 30.0% (214/713) described suicide-related content as contributing to suicidal thoughts or attempts, others reported relief, validation, or reduced feelings of isolation, with 21.0% (150/713) attributing content to preventing an attempt. Clear differences emerged between participants who actively sought out content (“seekers”) and those who encountered it unintentionally (“stumblers”). Seekers more frequently reported positive or understanding responses, often in the context of unmet offline support needs, whereas stumblers were more likely to report shock or distress. Approximately 39.9% (151/378) of participants described their engagement as neither intentional nor accidental, potentially reflecting a blurred boundary between passive exposure and active seeking, as well as the difficulty individuals face in accurately identifying and articulating their own motivations in relation to suicidality. Conclusions: Engagement with suicide-related online content cannot be characterized as uniformly harmful. Outcomes depend on user intent, emotional state, and the context of engagement, and they may change over time. Clinical, regulatory, and policy approaches should move beyond risk-only frameworks to account for the nuanced and sometimes supportive roles such content plays in how individuals make sense of suicidal thoughts, while still protecting those at risk.
title: Navigating Suicide-Related Online Content in Individuals With Lived Experience of Suicidality: Cross-Sectional Survey

summary: Background: Patients with cancer frequently experience complex and multidimensional symptom burdens. Standardized patient-reported outcome measures provide structured approaches to symptom assessment but may not capture the full range of symptom-related and psychosocial concerns expressed in patients’ narratives. Patient-generated social media data offer a complementary source for examining how these concerns are expressed online. Objective: This study aimed to characterize cancer symptom–related narratives in Chinese social media posts using a conventional symptom assessment framework and to identify additional experiential themes through neural topic modeling. Methods: A computational text analysis integrating large language model (LLM) annotation and neural topic modeling was conducted. A corpus of 26,086 first-person patient narratives was collected from Xiaohongshu and Zhihu between November 2013 and February 2026 using cancer-related search terms. First-person narratives and 6 SPPADE (sleep disturbance, pain, physical function impairment, anxiety, depression, and low energy or fatigue) symptom domains were identified using GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI) and validated against independent human coding. Symptom occurrence, co-occurrence, multiplicity, and coping strategies were characterized, with exploratory stratified analyses by cancer type. BERTopic modeling was applied to identify latent themes, platform sensitivity analyses, and temporal distribution were examined. Results: For first-person narrative identification, human raters showed 89.2% agreement (Cohen κ=0.784); the LLM achieved an -score of 81.2% against the adjudicated reference standard. For SPPADE extraction, mean Cohen κ values for LLM-human agreement were 0.714 (SD 0.114) and 0.754 (SD 0.095) across the 6 symptom domains. Overall, 13,896 of 26,086 (53.3%) posts contained at least 1 identifiable symptom. Pain was the most frequently identified symptom (5783/26,086, 22.2%), followed by physical function impairment (4153/26,086, 15.9%) and depression (4050/26,086, 15.5%). Pain and physical function impairment formed the most frequent co-occurring symptom pair (n=1407). Coping strategies were described in 7104/26,086 (27.2%) posts; medication-based approaches were most prominent, particularly for pain and sleep disturbance, while social and psychological support were more common for anxiety and depression. BERTopic modeling identified 13 latent themes, including cancer treatment trajectories, health care system interaction, existential distress, family involvement, and financial burden, highlighting experiential concerns that may be underrepresented in conventional symptom assessment. The proportion of posts containing at least 1 SPPADE symptom was similar between Xiaohongshu and Zhihu (53.2% vs 54.1%; =.35), although individual symptom distributions differed across platforms. Conclusions: Chinese social media posts contained multidimensional symptom-related narratives alongside psychosocial and experiential concerns that may be less visible in structured symptom assessment. Patient-generated social media data may therefore provide a complementary source for understanding cancer symptom experiences and supportive care concerns. However, differences in platform composition, uneven temporal coverage, and the nonrepresentativeness of social media users limit generalizability, and the clinical utility of integrating such data into routine symptom assessment requires further evaluation.
title: Characterizing Cancer Symptom Experiences and Related Psychosocial Concerns Through Chinese Social Media Narratives: Computational Text Analysis

summary: Background: Unemployment has economic consequences and is associated with emotional distress and impairment. Joblessness is often associated with depression, leading to a vicious cycle of reduced drive to seek work, deepening financial stress, and worsening depression. Few scalable interventions exist that integrate job-search strategies with cognitive behavioral techniques. Objective: The study aimed to determine the efficacy of a Distress-Informed Return-to-Work Intervention (DRIVEN). The primary hypothesis was that DRIVEN would be more efficacious than the control condition in improving job-search behavior. Secondary analyses examined job attainment, depression, and positive affect. Methods: A randomized controlled trial was conducted from August 2023 to September 2024. Assessments were at baseline, weeks 1 through 6, and 8 and 16 weeks postintervention. Participants were a nationwide sample of unemployed job seekers aged 18 years or older who had never earned more than US $100,000 in a year. Participants received either (1) DRIVEN, which included 6 weeks of cognitive behavioral exercises in a mobile app combined with three 1-hour coaching sessions over videoconference or (2) emailed articles containing job-search advice. Primary outcome measures were subscales of a modified Job Search Behavior Scale (preparatory and active job search). Secondary outcomes included job attainment and mental health outcomes. Results: Participants were a nationwide sample (N=126; mean age 33.6, SD 6.6 y), including 62 (49.2%) females. During the acute treatment phase, mixed-effects linear models showed that for DRIVEN, preparatory job-search behavior increased by an estimated 0.053 (95% CI 0.031-0.076) units per day from baseline, which was a larger effect than in the control condition (0.011, 95% CI −0.011 to 0.033 units per day; =.008). Active job-search behavior increased by 0.061 (95% CI 0.038-0.084) units per day from baseline, which was significantly larger than in the control group (point estimate: 0.025, 95% CI 0.001-0.047; =.03). Depression decreased more in the DRIVEN group vs control (DRIVEN point estimate=−0.214, 95% CI −0.255 to −0.172 vs control group point estimate=−0.122, 95% CI −0.163 to −0.081; =.002), and participants were more likely to get a job in the DRIVEN group (68.3% vs 50.8%; =.046). Self-report outcomes did not significantly differ during the follow-up periods. Conclusions: DRIVEN was superior to emailed job-search advice for the primary outcome (job-search behavior) and secondary outcomes (job attainment, depression, and positive affect). This intervention may be beneficial for distressed unemployed individuals seeking work. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06026280; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06026280 International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID): RR2-10.2196/62715
title: Job Coaching and Smartphone-Based Cognitive Behavioral Techniques for Returning to Work and Coping With Unemployment (DRIVEN): Randomized Controlled Trial

summary: Background: Clinical practice guidelines are central instruments of evidence-based care; yet, in many domains, particularly rare or complex diseases, multiple guidelines coexist and frequently offer conflicting advice. Existing strategies for resolving such divergences are often labor-intensive, opaque, and insufficiently reproducible. Objective: This tutorial aimed to develop and demonstrate a reproducible workflow for transforming divergent clinical guideline recommendations and literature-derived white areas into human-reviewed Delphi-ready candidate items. Methods: Following a step-by-step tutorial structure, we demonstrate the workflow using penile cancer as a worked example. The process comprises manual selection of clinical guidelines, a systematic PubMed search for literature-derived candidate issues potentially unaddressed by the selected guidelines, selection of 3 complementary large language models (LLMs), and execution of predefined prompts, multimodal recommendation extraction, semantic harmonization, and item-level guideline stance classification. The evaluative process combines a 3-LLM ensemble consistency check with an independent pre-Delphi appraisal by 4 penile cancer experts using a predefined 5-point suitability scale and acceptance threshold. Results: In the worked example in the field of penile cancer as a high-stakes use case, the workflow extracted 157 clinical recommendations from 5 guidelines and consolidated them into 68 harmonized guideline-derived items. Stance classification identified 15 uniformly supported items and 53 divergent, ambiguous, or incompletely addressed items. In parallel, literature processing generated 95 harmonized white-area items, of which 9 were classified as true white-area items not addressed by the included guidelines. The final methodological output was a set of 62 human-reviewed Delphi-ready candidate items for subsequent clinical consensus voting. Conclusions: This methodology provides a scalable, transparent, and transferable approach for identifying and structuring interguideline inconsistencies and evidence gaps. By combining LLM-assisted analysis with independent external expert appraisal, it supports the reproducible transformation of heterogeneous guideline content into Delphi-ready candidate items.
title: From Divergent Guidelines to Delphi-Ready Items: Tutorial for Large Language Model–Assisted Guideline Harmonization Using Penile Cancer as a Worked Example
